blocks.content: 1. INTRODUCTION TO TENSE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Tenses are broadly classified into three main types: Present, Past, and Future.
Each main tense category contains four specific forms: Simple, Continuous, Perfect, and Perfect Continuous.
Understanding specific time markers and verb forms is essential for identifying correct tense usage.
Mastering high-probability SSC rules helps in quickly identifying common errors in competitive examinations.

blocks.content:
Tense refers to the time at which an action takes place. It allows the reader to understand whether the action is happening now, has already happened, or will occur in the future.



Tense is one of the most important topics in English grammar because it directly affects sentence structure. In competitive examinations such as SSC, questions based on tense are frequently asked in Error Detection, Fill in the Blanks, Sentence Improvement, Active-Passive Voice, and Direct-Indirect Speech.



If the tense of a sentence is incorrect, the entire sentence becomes grammatically incorrect. Therefore, mastering tense is essential for scoring well in grammar sections.
2. CLASSIFICATION OF TENSE

English tense is divided into three main categories:



1. Present Tense – describes actions happening now or regularly.

2. Past Tense – describes actions that have already happened.

3. Future Tense – describes actions that will happen later.



Each tense has four sub-types:



• Simple / Indefinite

• Continuous

• Perfect

• Perfect Continuous



Thus, there are twelve tense structures in total.
3. PRESENT TENSE

Present tense describes actions occurring now, habitual actions, universal truths, and fixed arrangements.



Types of Present Tense:

• Present Indefinite

• Present Continuous

• Present Perfect

• Present Perfect Continuous
3.1 PRESENT INDEFINITE (SIMPLE PRESENT)

Uses:



1. Habitual actions:

She walks every morning.



2. Universal truths:

The earth revolves around the sun.



3. General facts:

Water boils at 100°C.



4. Scheduled events:

The train leaves at 6 a.m.



Structure:

Subject + V1 (add s/es with third person singular)



Negative:

Subject + do/does + not + V1



Interrogative:

Do/Does + subject + V1?



Important Rule:

Use “does” with he, she, it, or singular nouns.



Common Error:

Incorrect: He do not understand.

Correct: He does not understand.
3.2 PRESENT CONTINUOUS

This tense describes actions happening at the time of speaking.



Uses:

• Action happening now

• Temporary situations

• Planned near future



Example:

She is studying.



Structure:

Subject + is/am/are + V-ing



Stative Verbs:

Certain verbs are not used in continuous form because they describe a state rather than an action.



Examples include: know, believe, love, understand, own, belong.



Incorrect: I am knowing the answer.

Correct: I know the answer.
3.3 PRESENT PERFECT

The Present Perfect tense connects past actions with the present.



Uses:



1. Recently completed action:

She has finished her work.



2. Past action with present result:

I have lost my keys.



3. Life experiences:

I have visited Jaipur.



Structure:

Subject + has/have + V3



Rule:

Do not use definite past time expressions with Present Perfect.



Incorrect: I have seen him yesterday.

Correct: I saw him yesterday.
3.4 PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS

Used for actions that began in the past and are still continuing.



Example:

She has been studying for three hours.



Structure:

Subject + has/have + been + V-ing



Since vs For:

Since → starting point (since 2020)

For → duration (for two hours)



Incorrect: She is studying since morning.

Correct: She has been studying since morning.
4. PAST TENSE

Past tense describes actions that have already been completed.



Types:

• Simple Past

• Past Continuous

• Past Perfect

• Past Perfect Continuous
4.1 SIMPLE PAST

Used for actions completed at a definite time in the past.



Example:

He visited Delhi last year.



Structure:

Subject + V2



Negative:

Subject + did not + V1



Golden Rule:

After “did,” always use V1.



Incorrect: She did not went.

Correct: She did not go.
4.2 PAST CONTINUOUS

Describes an action that was in progress at a specific moment in the past.



Example:

I was watching television at 9 p.m.



Structure:

Subject + was/were + V-ing



Often used to show interruption:

I was sleeping when the phone rang.
4.3 PAST PERFECT

Used when two actions occurred in the past and we want to show which happened earlier.



Example:

The train had left before we reached.



Structure:

Subject + had + V3



Memory Rule:

Earlier action → Past Perfect

Later action → Simple Past
4.4 PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS

Emphasizes the duration of an action that was ongoing before another past action.



Example:

She had been working there for five years before she resigned.



Structure:

Subject + had been + V-ing

rows: Actions completed at a specific time in the past
Actions completed recently with a connection to the present
already, yet, recently, just, so far

blocks.content: 5. FUTURE TENSE

Future tense describes actions expected to happen later.



Types:

• Simple Future

• Future Continuous

• Future Perfect

• Future Perfect Continuous
5.1 SIMPLE FUTURE

Structure:

Subject + will + V1



Example:

She will succeed.



Modern English prefers “will” for most situations.
5.2 FUTURE CONTINUOUS

Describes an action that will be in progress at a specific time in the future.



Example:

This time tomorrow, I will be traveling to Chennai.



Structure:

Subject + will be + V-ing
5.3 FUTURE PERFECT

Used for actions that will be completed before a certain future time.



Example:

She will have finished the project by Monday.



Structure:

Subject + will have + V3
5.4 FUTURE PERFECT CONTINUOUS

The Future Perfect Continuous tense describes an action that will continue for a specific duration before a particular moment in the future.



It emphasizes both continuity and duration.



Example:

By next month, she will have been working here for five years.



Structure:

Subject + will have been + V-ing



When to Use:



1. To show duration before a future point:

By next week, he will have been studying for ten days.



2. To emphasize continuous effort:

By the time you arrive, we will have been waiting for three hours.



Common Mistake:

Incorrect: By next year, I will be working here for five years.

Correct: By next year, I will have been working here for five years.
6. HIGH-PROBABILITY SSC RULES

items: Do not use stative verbs (like know, love, believe, belong) in continuous tense forms.
Use 'since' to denote a specific point of time and 'for' to denote a duration of time in perfect continuous tenses.
Avoid using Simple Past when an action has relevance to the present time; use Present Perfect instead.

blocks.content:
1. After “did,” use V1.

2. After has/have/had, use V3.

3. Do not use Present Perfect with past time expressions.

4. Use Past Perfect when two past actions are mentioned.

5. Modal verbs are always followed by V1.



Special Rule:

After “It is time” or “It is high time,” use V2.



Incorrect: It is time you go.

Correct: It is time you went.
7. COMMON ERRORS IN EXAMINATIONS

Incorrect: He has completed the work yesterday.

Correct: He completed the work yesterday.



Incorrect: I am understanding the problem.

Correct: I understand the problem.



Incorrect: She did not wrote the letter.

Correct: She did not write the letter.
8. PRACTICE QUESTIONS (SSC LEVEL)

Error Detection:



1. He has finished the report last night.

2. She did not went to college.

3. I am believing your story.



Fill in the blanks:



1. She ______ already ______ the assignment. (has / complete)

2. They ______ playing when I arrived. (was / were)

3. The movie ______ before we reached the theatre. (start)



Answers:

1. has completed

2. were

3. had started
9. QUICK REVISION SUMMARY

Present → V1 / is-ing / has V3

Past → V2 / was-ing / had V3

Future → will V1 / will be-ing / will have V3



Remember:

Correct tense ensures clarity, accuracy, and grammatical correctness.
